items.headline: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'
items.blurb: The Ukrainian president says the slowed-down internet is making it difficult to stop Russian attacks.
items.text: A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. "We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said. The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military-grade Starlink service owned by Elon Musk and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks. Zelensky said he had asked officials "to work as closely as possible" with the US government and Musk's company. "It is important to be on the right side of history," he said. The BBC has asked the White House and Starlink for comment. Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones in Ukraine airspace. items.headline: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
items.blurb: After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’ The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded…
items.text: After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’ The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation. Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter , which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October. Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement : “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. items.headline: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
items.blurb: The Nvidia scandal has raised questions over whether advanced AI chips ended up in China, despite US restrictions.
items.text: Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees. Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business. Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence". It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". items.headline: Founder of Guadalajara cartel dies in hospital after decades in prison
items.blurb: Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo was convicted of the 1985 murder of a US drug enforcement agent and a Mexican pilot.
items.text: Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the founder of one of Mexico’s first major drug cartels, has died in hospital at age 80. Local security authorities said Felix Gallardo was transferred to a private hospital in the western city of Guadalajara two days ago but suffered multiple organ failure and died at about 2pm (20:00 GMT) on Sunday. Felix Gallardo, a founder of the Guadalajara cartel, was convicted for the 1985 killing of a US drug-enforcement agent, a crime that made him one of the country’s most notorious traffickers. Imprisoned since 1989, Felix Gallardo was held in a maximum-security prison in western Jalisco state, though his lawyers repeatedly sought house arrest on the grounds of his deteriorating health. Rising to prominence in the 1970s, the former cartel kingpin was an architect of Mexico’s modern drug-trafficking trade, igniting a series of turf wars that have led to hundreds of thousands of deaths and disappearances in the ensuing decades. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October. items.text: Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80. Félix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smugglers in history and is credited with building an alliance between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel. Known as The Godfather or the 'Boss of Bosses', Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s. At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989. The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's. He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States. items.headline: After a nationwide ground stop, US faces aviation infrastructure questions
items.blurb: Trump has requested $50bn for upgrades, but Democratic lawmakers are asking for transparency before spending more.
items.text: Last Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounded all flights in the United States for nearly four hours due to a reported equipment failure. It was only the second time since the attacks on September 11, 2001, that such an order was given. More than 9,000 flights were cancelled, and an estimated 1.5 million passengers were left stranded. Officials blamed the disruptions on an upgrade gone awry. The routers used to communicate with aeroplanes in mid-flight had suddenly stopped working , and pilots were no longer able to speak on their usual frequencies. As of Sunday, officials were still working to return the system to normal. “As we look to the end of the day and into tomorrow, we should be running at full capacity,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CBS News, while acknowledging continued delays. But the situation has led to scrutiny over whether the nationwide ground-stop could have been prevented. items.blurb: President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.
items.text: President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said. The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry. An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said. The health ministry gave the casualty toll, adding more than 70 of the injured were discharged after receiving treatment. Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways. items.headline: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
items.blurb: Han Won-seok, 34, confessed to using a hidden camera and AI to get a near-perfect mark on the significant test.
items.text: A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools. Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated. The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation. Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance. "I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday. "I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating." items.headline: Government may call Parliament winter session in early December
items.blurb: Opposition parties say the government has not shared the schedule and are protesting the electoral-roll revision.
items.text: The winter session of Parliament is likely to begin in the first week of December, with the Constitution amendment bill linked to delimitation and women’s reservation among the key legislative priorities of the Centre, even as Opposition parties said on Sunday that they had received no communication from the government on the proposed schedule People familiar with the discussions said the first week of December was emerging as the likely window, with possible dates discussed at the highest levels of the government. The monsoon session, whose last working day was August 13, has not yet been prorogued. The government can either prorogue it and convene a fresh session or extend the existing session at short notice. A fresh session requires the President to summon Parliament, with lawmakers generally receiving at least a couple of weeks’ notice, while an extension of the existing session does not require a fresh summons. items.headline: US FAA begins 5-day audit of DGCA’s safety oversight system
items.blurb: The assessment, scheduled from November 16 to 20, is being conducted under the FAA’s International Aviation Safety Assessment programme.
items.text: The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) will begin reassessing India’s aviation safety oversight system from Monday, officials said. A team is scheduled to examine the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) over five days, focusing on its aircraft operations, airworthiness and personnel licensing processes. The assessment, scheduled from November 16 to 20, is being conducted under the FAA’s International Aviation Safety Assessment (IASA) programme. This programme evaluates whether a country’s civil aviation regulator complies with safety standards set by the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO), a specialised agency of the United Nations. “The FAA looks at airworthiness, safety, operations and licensing. We are confident India will retain the Category 1 status this year too,” an official said, on the condition of anonymity. India was last assessed in 2021, when its ICAO effective implementation (EI) score rose from 69.95% to 85.65%, indicating improved compliance with international aviation safety standards. India currently holds Category 1 status under the FAA’s IASA programme. items.blurb: The weather system is likely to become a Severe Cyclonic Storm over the westcentral Bay of Bengal by the evening of November 17, the IMD said.
items.text: A depression over the Bay of Bengal is likely to strengthen into a cyclonic storm by the evening of November 16 and further intensify into a severe cyclonic storm by November 17, before moving towards the Andhra Pradesh coast over the following two days, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said on Sunday. The weather system is expected to move north-northwestwards as it gains strength over the central parts of the south and adjoining west central Bay of Bengal. It is likely to become a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal by the evening of November 17, the IMD said. items.headline: Embattled Jensen Huang is discussing comeback as Nvidia CEO amid mounting pressure on board to reinstate him: Report
items.blurb: A campaign is reportedly building to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO days after his resignation amid relationship allegations. Tech executives, investors and employees have voiced support, and allies are seeking White House backing. Nvidia’s board is still in the process of choosing a new CEO.
items.text: On November 12, Jensen Huang was forced to step down as CEO of Nvidia, the company he co-founded and led since its inception in 1993, in one of the most polarizing moves in recent corporate history. But just days after his ouster, Huang is already plotting his comeback to the helm of the world’s second-most valuable company. According to The Financial Times , Huang is discussing a return to Nvidia as CEO with some of his closest allies. A Huang ally told FT that they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief’s return and would try to garner support from the White House. “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the ally said, adding that “The efforts had Huang’s support.” According to a Financial Times report, Huang is discussing a possible return with some of his closest allies. His reinstatement has not been confirmed. Huang’s allies are reportedly organizing a group of Silicon Valley executives to support his return and seek backing from the White House.

items.blurb: GLOBAL-PRECIOUS:Gold edges higher as investors await Warsh remarks for rate signals
items.text: Nov 16 (Reuters) - Gold prices edged higher in early Asian trade on Monday after last week's more-than-one-year low, as investors awaited remarks from Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh for clues to the outlook for US interest rates. Spot gold was up 0.3% at $3,892.42 per ounce by 0050 GMT, while US gold futures for December delivery rose 0.2% to $3,895.60. Bullion dropped 4.5% last week, pressured by rising oil prices that fuelled inflation concerns and reinforced expectations of higher for longer interest rates. US producer prices rose further in October, posting the biggest annual gain in four years and reinforcing expectations that the Fed could continue raising rates after a widely expected hike next month. Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid said on Sunday that inflation was still "running too hot" and that the central bank had "some work to do" to bring price pressures under control. items.headline: UK will have 'voice' but no vote on EU food rules in Brexit reset
items.blurb: EU minister Hamish Falconer insists Britain would have some influence on policy as part of a new deal.
items.text: The UK will have a "voice in the room" but no vote on European Union food policies as part of a so-called "Brexit reset" to reduce red tape, EU relations minister Hamish Falconer has told the BBC. Prime Minister Andy Burnham hopes to agree a deal at a summit on Friday but critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker" but not a rule maker. Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules and said the deal could help bring down prices for shoppers. The reset would not involve any upfront payments, Falconer added, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment. Falconer said it was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. items.text: Ola Electric's cash reserves have dwindled 87% from ₹ 5,918 crore a month after its stock market debut to ₹ 750 crore a little over two years later. Bhavish Aggarwal’s electric scooter maker has seen an average monthly cash depletion of ₹ 215 crore over the period, as sales declined and the former market leader slid to fifth place. Revenue continued to decline for the eighth consecutive quarter in July-September, while fresh capital raised through a qualified institutional placement (QIP) of shares in June and a rights issue in October has done little to arrest the company's financial deterioration. The company had raised ₹ 5,500 crore through its initial public offering (IPO) in August 2024, and ₹ 780 crore through the QIP in June this year to bulk up its cash reserves. While the company's October rights issue of ₹ 1,000 crore, of which it has raised about ₹ 600 crore so far, will support its balance sheet, its existing loans of nearly ₹ 1,800 crore and rising quarterly losses mean its financial outlook remains uncertain. items.text: While India’s travel market continues to expand despite geopolitical disruptions, elevated airfares and capacity constraints, Yatra’s latest results highlight the challenge of converting booking growth into sustainable earnings Bookings grew, but revenue shrank and profit disappeared. That was the paradox of Yatra in the September quarter, when India’s travel tech sector was expected to capture the momentum leading into the festive and holiday travel season. The listed travel tech company reported a consolidated net loss of ₹78.4 Lakh in Q2 FY27, against a net profit of ₹14.3 Cr in the year-ago period. Revenue from operations declined 39.1% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹213.6 Cr, reflecting a slowdown in its ‘Meetings, Incentives, Conferences and Exhibitions’ (MICE) business, which has historically contributed meaningfully to its corporate travel operations. Yatra’s results have come at a precarious time. Its US-listed parent, Yatra Online, has received a notice from the Nasdaq for failing to maintain the exchange’s minimum $1 closing bid-price requirement. The company's revenue from operations increased to Rs 2,396 crore in Q2 FY27 from Rs 2,099 crore in the corresponding quarter last year. On a quarterly basis, FirstCry's revenue from operations increased 13.8% to Rs 2,396 crore in Q2 FY27 from Rs 2,106 crore in Q1 FY27. The Pune-based company also recorded Rs 42 crore in other income, pushing its total income to Rs 2,438 crore in Q2 FY27. On the expense front, material procurement remained the largest expense head, rising 16.9% year-on-year to Rs 1,554 crore in Q2 FY27 from Rs 1,329 crore in the corresponding quarter last year. Employee benefit expenses declined 10.8% to Rs 181 crore from Rs 203 crore in Q2 FY26. Meanwhile, depreciation expenses fell 1.5% to Rs 97 crore, while finance costs also declined to Rs 39 crore during the quarter. Other expenses increased 12.6% year-on-year to Rs 568 crore in Q2 FY27

First of all the context of the two games was entirely different. England were 1–0 up against Argentina in the 55th minute on neutral territory in Atlanta - and still had all their players. items.blurb: Apple announced a new study today with the goal of better understanding how people interact with conversational AI health tools and how useful their responses actually are.
items.text: The study will be conducted through a new app where participants can ask health questions and rate the responses. The study will be conducted through a new app where participants can ask health questions and rate the responses. Apple announced a new study today with the goal of better understanding how people interact with conversational AI health tools and how useful their responses actually are. The company is conducting the Apple Health AI Usage Study in collaboration with OpenEvidence , a clinical AI platform used by healthcare professionals that generates answers based on medical information from sources like The New England Journal of Medicine . Participants will use a new iOS app to ask medical questions and then rate the responses based on criteria including accuracy, detail, and relevance. The app is now available for download, and enrollment starts today, with Apple looking for up to 200,000 people to contribute. Participants 21 and older must be based in the US, and although the app doesn’t use Apple Intelligence, it does require an iPhone 15 Pro running iOS 26 or later.

items.text: The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment. “After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10. items.text: If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US , it’s reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week , Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, “I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident.” In the opening lecture of a three-part series , Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending “AI takeover.” He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems “call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth” and where any human trying to stop them “would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military.” Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said. items.headline: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Hydrogen, finally replacing 3.8 Flash
items.blurb: Gemini 4 Hydrogen isn't getting a slow, security-conscious release like Carbon and Argon.
items.text: Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen . These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen’s purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google’s ecosystem use. Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it’s 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces “fabricated claims” by more than 5x, according to Google’s analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash’s score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon. Google believes Hydrogen will be a key part of how developers work with agentic coding tools. items.headline: Innovating with AI in the special chemicals industry
items.blurb: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market.
items.text: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance. Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. items.text: I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons , even if just for an hour. I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets. items.headline: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
items.blurb: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially…
items.text: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.”

items.headline: Is bad news for Jensen Huang also bad news for the AI industry?
items.blurb: "Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia."
items.text: We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.” “Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.” Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return .) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem. items.text: As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. items.text: CHICAGO—Families joined protests in seven cities nationwide on Wednesday, rallying against what they see as Google’s bid to entrench its AI models in schools, turn kids of all ages into Gemini guinea pigs, and hook them on AI. The backlash follows a Google statement last week, confirming that there will be no way for students to use Google Search without AI. While Google claimed it was giving schools “more choice, not less”—by turning off Search, Gemini, and Gemini Notebook by default—it would not provide an option that allowed Search without AI. For students, the only way to avoid interacting with AI was to remember to add “-ai” to every query, parents worried. In Chicago, many families showed up to protest Google, despite cold, rainy weather. Waving signs, dozens of protesters marched up to Google’s downtown office as workers seemed to be leaving for the day, shouting chants like “Hey Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini” and “Hey, Google, leave our kids alone!” Called to action by a nonprofit grassroots advocacy group, the Illinois Families for Public Schools (ILFPS),

Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. items.text: NVIDIA’s influence in India extends far beyond GPU sales, spanning AI infrastructure, software, developer ecosystems, startup incubation and direct equity investments. With Indian data centre operators committing billions of dollars to NVIDIA-powered infrastructure, and enterprises and startups building on its CUDA-led software stack, the company has become deeply embedded in the country's AI ambitions. As Jensen Huang exits, the bigger question is whether India can reduce its dependence on a single technology provider, particularly as geopolitical uncertainties, export restrictions and competing chip architectures reshape access to AI compute. Jensen Huang’s exit from NVIDIA has put the spotlight on the company’s leadership and succession plans. But for India, the more consequential question is what happens to an ecosystem that has increasingly come to depend on the American chipmaker for its AI ambitions. From data centre operators ordering thousands of GPUs to startups building on its software stack, NVIDIA has established relationships across almost every layer of India’s AI industry.
